name: Color Quantization Error Analysis
description: Analyzes the error patterns produced when an image's colors are quantized (reduced) to a smaller palette. Real photographs processed through standard ADC (analog-to-digital conversion) produce specific quantization error patterns governed by sensor bit depth and gamma encoding. AI-generated images exhibit different quantization characteristics because their pixel values originate from neural network floating-point computations rounded to integer values.
algorithm: Optimal Palette Quantization Error Distribution Analysis
mechanism:
Color quantization maps a continuous color space to a finite set of representative colors. The error between the original and quantized values follows predictable patterns: (1) **Uniform quantization** from camera ADCs produces uniformly distributed errors within each quantization bin. (2) **Perceptual quantization** (gamma encoding) produces non-uniform bin widths — darker values have finer bins than bright values.

The detector quantizes the input image using median-cut or k-means algorithms (k = 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 palette sizes) and analyzes the error residuals at each palette size. The forensic signals are:

• **Error distribution shape** — authentic camera images produce residuals matching the expected gamma-encoded uniform distribution. AI images show modal peaks in the error histogram corresponding to common neural network output values (often concentrated near 0, 127, 255 in 8-bit).
• **Error spatial correlation** — in real photos, quantization error is spatially uncorrelated (white noise). AI generators produce spatially correlated quantization errors because neighboring pixels are computed from similar latent vectors.
• **Palette efficiency** — real photographs typically require 200+ colors to reduce quantization error below 2 LSB (least significant bit). AI images often show anomalously low error with far fewer colors because their effective color diversity is lower than natural scenes.
parameters:
Quantization method: median-cut + k-means refinement
Palette sizes tested: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256 colors
Error metric: per-pixel L2 distance in CIELAB space
Spatial correlation test: Moran's I autocorrelation index
Palette efficiency: colors needed for RMSE < 2 LSB
Scoring: combined z-score across all palette levels
accuracy: Moderate — 65-75% accuracy. Most effective on images with wide color gamut; less discriminative on images dominated by limited color palettes (e.g., graphics, logos).
source: Orchard, M.T. & Bouman, C.A. (1991). Color Quantization of Images. IEEE TSP.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated images through analysis of their color palette structure, identifying images with artificially limited color diversity, forensic analysis of color space utilization, and complementary signal for ensemble AI detection pipelines.
strengths:
• Captures fundamental differences in how cameras vs. neural networks produce pixel values
• The palette efficiency metric provides an intuitive and interpretable forensic measure
• Multi-palette analysis (different k values) creates a robust feature set
• Fast computation using optimized quantization algorithms
limitations:
• Graphics, illustrations, and screenshots naturally have limited palettes — causing false positives
• Heavy JPEG compression introduces its own quantization artifacts that mask the original signal
• Modern AI generators with dithering or noise injection can approximate natural quantization error patterns
• Images captured with reduced bit depth (e.g., some phone cameras) show different baselines

references.title: Orchard, M.T. & Bouman, C.A. (1991). Color Quantization of Images. IEEE TSP.
Heckbert, P. (1982). Color Image Quantization for Frame Buffer Display. ACM SIGGRAPH.
